new.title: Find the Smiling Angel on Reims cathedral
new.desc: Begun in 1211, Notre-Dame de Reims is where French kings were crowned for centuries, Charles VII among them in 1429 with Joan of Arc at his side. On the west front, a sculpted angel with a famous half smile was decapitated by a burning beam when the cathedral caught fire under German shelling in September 1914, then pieced back together in 1926. Inside, the axial chapel glows with blue stained glass designed by Marc Chagall in 1974.
new.tip: The Smiling Angel is on the left-hand (north) portal of the west facade, so look up before you go in. In late spring the city's Joan of Arc festival fills the streets around the cathedral with parades and a medieval market.

new.title: Visit the tomb of Saint Remi in his Romanesque basilica
new.desc: This long, light-filled abbey church, largely 11th century, was built around the tomb of Saint Remi, the bishop who baptised Clovis, king of the Franks. Together with the cathedral and the Palais du Tau it was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991.
new.tip: It is a 20-minute walk south of the cathedral and usually far quieter. Pair it with the Musée Saint-Remi next door in the old abbey buildings.

new.title: Explore Roman and medieval Reims at the Musée Saint-Remi
new.desc: The city's history museum fills the former royal abbey of Saint-Remi beside the basilica, with a grand staircase from 1778 and a 12th-century chapter house. Its star piece is the marble sarcophagus of Jovinus, a Roman cavalry commander from Reims, said to be the finest ancient marble sarcophagus in France.
new.tip: Combine it with the basilica on the same visit. A good choice for a wet afternoon in the Saint-Remi quarter.

new.title: Stand under the Porte de Mars, a Roman triumphal arch
new.desc: Built in the early 3rd century AD at the northern entrance of Roman Durocortorum, this three-bayed arch is 32 metres long, said to be the widest arch in the Roman world. It survived because it was folded into a medieval castle and then the city walls, which were only cleared away in the 1850s.
new.tip: Look up into the vaults: worn reliefs show farm work, Leda and the swan, and Romulus and Remus with the she-wolf. It sits on the edge of the Hautes Promenades, so it is an easy stop between the station and the Halles du Boulingrin.

new.title: Step down into the Roman galleries of the Cryptoportique
new.desc: On Place du Forum, a half-buried vaulted gallery is what remains of the forum of Roman Durocortorum, the ancestor of Reims. It has been listed as a historic monument since 1923.
new.tip: It is open for free self-guided visits in summer, usually daily from 2 to 6 pm. In July and August there are often evening concerts in front of it.

new.title: See the room where the Second World War ended in Europe
new.desc: At 2:41 am on 7 May 1945, General Jodl signed Germany's unconditional surrender in a school building that served as Eisenhower's headquarters. The map room has been kept exactly as it was, with the Allied operations maps still covering the walls.
new.tip: The museum is small, so allow about an hour. It is a short walk from the station, behind the Lycée Roosevelt.

new.title: Tour the Art Nouveau Villa Demoiselle
new.desc: Architect Louis Sorel built this villa opposite the Pommery estate between 1904 and 1908 for Henry Vasnier, Pommery's director, who died before it was finished. Abandoned for years, it was rescued by the Vranken family and painstakingly restored, reopening to visitors in 2008.
new.tip: Visits are booked through Vranken-Pommery, and a combined ticket with the Pommery cellars across the road is good value.

new.title: See Foujita's frescoes in his little chapel
new.desc: The Japanese-French painter Léonard Tsuguharu Foujita designed this Romanesque-style chapel and painted every wall himself, consecrated in October 1966. It was paid for by René Lalou, head of Mumm and Foujita's godfather, and the artist is buried inside.
new.tip: It only opens from early May to the end of September and closes on Tuesdays. It sits right next to the Mumm cellars, so combine the two.

new.title: Walk through the Fort de la Pompelle, Reims' WWI shield
new.desc: Built in 1880 to 1883 on the southeastern edge of Reims, this fort was retaken by French troops in September 1914 and never fell again, despite constant shelling and three assaults in 1918, one of them with tanks. Today it is a museum of the Great War, famous for its collection of German imperial helmets and headgear, said to be unique in the world.
new.tip: You need a car or bike to get there, on the road towards Châlons. Walk the trenches and shell craters outside too, they are still clearly visible.

new.title: Admire the Art Deco hall of the Carnegie Library
new.desc: After the First World War the Carnegie Foundation paid to rebuild the municipal library of battered Reims. Designed by Max Sainsaulieu and built between 1920 and 1927, it is an Art Deco jewel of mosaics, wrought iron, bas-reliefs and glass.
new.tip: It is a working public library, so entry is free during opening hours. Keep your voice down and look up at the glass ceiling of the hall.

new.title: Stroll Place Drouet-d'Erlon from fountain to café
new.desc: The long square named after Marshal Drouet d'Erlon, born in Reims, is the city's living room. Almost entirely destroyed in the First World War, it was rebuilt with Art Deco facades, went largely pedestrian in 1993, and has the Subé fountain, topped by a statue of Glory, at its centre.
new.tip: Come at aperitif time on a sunny evening, when every terrace is full. Head to the side streets for better value than on the square itself.

new.title: Discover Dürer prints at the Musée Le Vergeur
new.desc: This merchant's mansion on Place du Forum, with parts dating to the 13th century, was the home of the collector Hugues Krafft, who left it to the city. Among its treasures are Albrecht Dürer's complete Apocalypse and Large Passion series of woodcuts, plus period rooms and a pretty garden.
new.tip: Opening is mostly in the afternoon and some visits are guided, so check the Reims museums site before you go. The Cryptoportique and Le Wine Bar are on the same square.

new.title: See Vieira da Silva's windows in Saint-Jacques church
new.desc: Tucked among the shopping streets, Saint-Jacques is the oldest surviving church in Reims after Saint-Remi. Its medieval walls hold modern abstract stained glass: windows by the Czech painter Joseph Sima from the 1960s and by Maria Helena Vieira da Silva, installed in 1996 and 1997.
new.tip: Go in on a sunny afternoon, when the windows come alive. It is two minutes from Place Drouet-d'Erlon.

new.title: Shop for Reims ham and cheese at the Halles du Boulingrin
new.desc: Under a thin concrete vault from 1929 by Émile Maigrot and Eugène Freyssinet, the city's covered market is one of the great Art Deco buildings of Reims. Saved from demolition and restored, it reopened in 2012 and is packed with cheesemongers, butchers, fishmongers and champagne stalls.
new.tip: The full market runs on Wednesday, Friday and Saturday mornings, and Saturday is liveliest. Look for jambon de Reims, a pressed ham set in parsley jelly, and the oyster stands.

new.title: Dunk a pink biscuit at Maison Fossier
new.desc: The biscuit rose de Reims is a crisp, twice-baked sponge finger coloured pink with carmine, made here since the late 17th century. Maison Fossier, founded in 1756, is the last historic maker in town and still sells them by the box.
new.tip: Locals dip them in champagne or a glass of red wine. The shop on Cours Jean-Baptiste Langlet is right in the centre, and the boxes travel well as gifts.
new.q: Biscuits Fossier, Cours Jean-Baptiste Langlet, Reims

new.title: Take tea in the Art Deco salon of Pâtisserie Waïda
new.desc: On Place Drouet-d'Erlon, the Waïda family's pâtisserie and tea room has kept its period interior of mosaics, mirrors and marble counters. It is a classic Reims stop for breakfast, pastries and chocolates.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays. Sit inside rather than at the counter to enjoy the decor.
new.q: Waïda et Fils, Place Drouet d'Erlon, Reims

new.title: Order seafood at the Brasserie du Boulingrin
new.desc: Opened in 1925, this Art Deco brasserie faces the covered market it is named after and still serves the full classic repertoire: oyster platters, choucroute, steak tartare and champagne by the glass. Locals and visitors share the same packed dining room.
new.tip: Book at weekends, especially on Saturday after the market. The set menu at lunch is the best value.
new.q: Le Boulingrin, 31 Rue de Mars, Reims

new.title: Sip champagne under the glass roof of the Café du Palais
new.desc: Run by the same family since 1930, this café opposite the Grand Théâtre is crammed with paintings, posters and curios. Above it all is an Art Deco glass roof by the Reims master glassmaker Jacques Simon.
new.tip: Order a coupe of champagne with a slice of their homemade tart at tea time. It is closed on Sundays.
new.q: Café du Palais, Place Myron Herrick, Reims

new.title: Splurge on three-star cooking at L'Assiette Champenoise
new.desc: Arnaud Lallement's family restaurant on the western edge of Reims has held three Michelin stars since 2014 and kept them in the 2026 guide. His cooking is precise and produce-led, with a famous blue lobster and a deep champagne list.
new.tip: Book weeks ahead. Lunch menus are the gentlest way into the experience, and Tinqueux is a short taxi or tram-and-walk from the centre.
new.q: L'Assiette Champenoise, Avenue Paul Vaillant-Couturier, Tinqueux

new.title: Taste the Widow's champagne at Veuve Clicquot
new.desc: Barbe-Nicole Ponsardin took over her late husband's house in 1805, at 27, and turned it into a powerhouse. Her team invented the riddling table that clears champagne of its sediment, and in 1818 she made the first known blended rosé.
new.tip: Tours of the chalk pits fill up fast in summer, so book online well in advance. Reception is on Place des Droits de l'Homme.

new.title: Try grower champagnes at Le Wine Bar on Place du Forum
new.desc: Run by the Papavero brothers of the Le Vintage wine shop, this bar on Place du Forum pours champagnes from small growers alongside the big names. It regularly features in guides to the best wine bars in Champagne.
new.tip: Ask for a flight comparing two or three villages. A board of local charcuterie and cheese goes well with it.
new.q: Le Wine Bar, 16 Place du Forum, Reims

new.title: Descend into the Ruinart chalk pits
new.desc: Founded in 1729 by Nicolas Ruinart, nephew of a Benedictine monk, Ruinart is the oldest established champagne house. Its cellars are vast chalk quarries on the Saint-Nicaise hill, part of the Champagne hillsides, houses and cellars listed by UNESCO in 2015.
new.tip: Tours are small and pricey, so book well ahead. The house is famous for its blanc de blancs, so taste a chardonnay-based cuvée.
new.q: Maison Ruinart, Rue des Crayères, Reims

new.title: Walk 116 steps down into the Pommery cellars
new.desc: Jeanne Alexandrine Pommery turned ancient chalk pits into 18 km of galleries in the 1870s, with an extravagant neo-Elizabethan estate on top. Her house launched one of the first brut champagnes in 1874, and today the cellars double as a contemporary art gallery.
new.tip: Bring a warm layer: it is about 10°C underground all year. The grand staircase down is 116 steps, so count them on the way back up.
new.q: Champagne Pommery, Boulevard Henry Vasnier, Reims

new.title: Explore the abbey crypts under Taittinger
new.desc: Taittinger's cellars lie beneath the site of the 13th-century Saint-Nicaise abbey, where monks once kept their wine. Further down, 4th-century Gallo-Roman chalk pits shelter millions of bottles.
new.tip: The house is a five-minute walk from the Basilique Saint-Remi. Weekday morning tours are the least crowded.

new.title: Tour the Mumm cellars, home of Cordon Rouge
new.desc: Founded in 1827 by the Mumm brothers, German winemakers from the Rhine valley, the house is known for Cordon Rouge, whose red ribbon imitates the sash of the Legion of Honour. The tour leads through the cellars on Rue du Champ de Mars, past old presses and dusty reserve bottles.
new.tip: The Foujita chapel is next door and was built thanks to a Mumm chairman. Book online for the cheapest tour slot.

new.title: Start in the vines at Lanson's walled Clos
new.desc: Founded in 1760, Lanson is one of the oldest champagne houses. Its tour begins in the Clos Lanson, a single plot of chardonnay inside the city, then moves through the vat house, wood cellar and chalk galleries.
new.tip: Allow two hours for the full visit. The shop does walk-in tastings without a booking if you are short on time.

new.title: Warm up with mulled champagne at the Christmas market
new.desc: Reims runs one of the biggest Christmas markets in France, with rows of wooden chalets on the Hautes Promenades. In 2026 it is open from 25 November to 27 December.
new.tip: On Friday and Saturday evenings, stay for the Regalia light show projected on the cathedral facade.

new.title: Cycle the Coulée Verte along the Reims canal
new.desc: An 18 km car-free greenway follows the Canal de l'Aisne à la Marne straight through Reims, from La Neuvillette in the north to Sillery in the south. Open since 2008, it has a smooth paved lane for bikes and skates.
new.tip: Ride south towards Sillery and you are soon among the first vineyards of the Montagne de Reims. Reims has bike hire near the station.

new.title: Picnic in the Parc de Champagne
new.desc: The Marquis de Polignac of Pommery laid out this 21-hectare park from 1909 as a place of leisure and sport for the cellar workers, and it was first known as the Parc Pommery. Today its lawns, old trees and play areas make a peaceful break between cellar visits.
new.tip: Pick up picnic supplies at the Halles du Boulingrin on a market morning and bring them here.

new.title: Walk the Avenue de Champagne in Épernay
new.desc: Lined with the mansions of Moët & Chandon, Perrier-Jouët, Pol Roger, de Venoge and others, this avenue sits on top of kilometres of chalk cellars holding millions of bottles. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2015 as part of the Champagne hillsides, houses and cellars.
new.tip: Walk it end to end, then pick a house for a visit. Many have tasting rooms you can enter without booking.

new.title: Visit Dom Pérignon's grave in Hautvillers
new.desc: The monk Dom Pierre Pérignon was cellar master at the Benedictine abbey of Hautvillers until his death in 1715 and is buried in its church. The hilltop village above the Marne valley is full of wrought-iron signs showing wine-making scenes.
new.tip: The abbey itself belongs to Moët & Chandon and is closed, but the church is open. Walk to the viewpoint at the edge of the village for the classic vineyard panorama.
new.q: Église Saint-Pierre, Rue de l'Abbaye, Hautvillers

new.title: Wander among the twisted beeches of the Faux de Verzy
new.desc: In the Verzy forest on the Montagne de Reims grow about a thousand dwarf beeches with contorted, umbrella-shaped crowns, the largest concentration of these tortuous trees in the world. The site has been protected since 1932, and a marked trail keeps visitors off their fragile roots.
new.tip: Come in winter when the leaves are gone to see the twisted branches best. Look for the 'Fau parapluie', the umbrella beech.

new.title: Climb a lighthouse in the middle of the vineyards
new.desc: This lighthouse far from any sea was built in 1909 as an advertisement for the champagne house Joseph Goulet. Since 1999 it has housed a museum of the vine, and 101 steps lead to a platform 25 metres up with a 360° view over the grand cru vineyards.
new.tip: Go at sunset in late summer, when the vines are heavy with grapes. A gentle walk on the vineyard paths below is free.

new.title: Hear the 56 bells of Notre-Dame-en-Vaux in Châlons
new.desc: This Romanesque and Gothic collegiate church on the canals of Châlons-en-Champagne is a UNESCO World Heritage Site on the pilgrim routes to Santiago de Compostela. Its towers hold one of the largest carillons in Europe, and its demolished cloister lives on in a museum of remarkable carved columns next door.
new.tip: Carillon concerts take place regularly in summer. The cloister museum is small but the statue-columns are outstanding.

new.title: Spot the gargoyles of L'Épine basilica
new.desc: This flamboyant Gothic basilica, built from 1406 to 1527 in a tiny village, has the size of a cathedral. Legend says shepherds found a statue of the Virgin in a burning thorn bush here, and the church is now a UNESCO site on the routes to Santiago.
new.tip: Walk around the outside slowly: the gargoyles include monsters, drunkards and even a wolf. It is just 8 km east of Châlons.

new.title: Stand by the windmill where the Revolution was saved
new.desc: On 20 September 1792 French revolutionary troops under Kellermann halted the Prussian army at Valmy, and the next day the Republic was proclaimed. The windmill on the ridge was rebuilt in 2005 after a storm destroyed its predecessor, and a museum about the battle opened beneath it in 2014.
new.tip: The hilltop is free to visit and the views over the Champagne plain are wide. Look for the statue of Kellermann nearby.

new.title: Count the stone oxen on Laon cathedral
new.desc: Built mainly between about 1160 and 1230 on a hilltop that rises above the plain, Laon cathedral is one of the most unified early Gothic churches in France. Sixteen life-size stone oxen peer out from its towers, said to honour the animals that hauled stone up the hill.
new.tip: Use binoculars or a zoom lens for the oxen. The tourist office runs guided tours up the towers in season.

new.title: Walk the ramparts and gates of Laon's upper town
new.desc: Medieval walls still wrap around Laon's long ridge, pierced by fortified gates such as the Porte d'Ardon. A walk along the ramparts gives views over the plain of Picardy and back to the cathedral towers.
new.tip: Start at the Porte d'Ardon and follow the promenade around the hill. Wear good shoes, as the lanes and stairways are steep.

new.title: Explore the ruins of Coucy, once Europe's mightiest keep
new.desc: Enguerrand III de Coucy built this castle around 1225 to 1240, with a keep 54 metres tall and over 30 metres wide, the largest in medieval Europe. Retreating German troops blew it up with 28 tonnes of explosives on 27 March 1917, with no military reason.
new.tip: Walk the medieval town walls of Coucy-le-Château as well. The scale of the keep's broken base gives a sense of how huge it was.

new.title: Go underground at the Caverne du Dragon
new.desc: This medieval quarry under the Chemin des Dames was fought over by French and German troops for most of the First World War, sometimes shared by both at once. The Germans called it the Dragon's Cave because of the machine-gun fire spitting from its entrances. It is now the Chemin des Dames museum.
new.tip: Visits are guided and bookable, and it stays cold underground. Drive along the Chemin des Dames ridge afterwards to see its memorials.

new.title: Pay respects at the Aisne-Marne American Cemetery
new.desc: At the foot of Belleau Wood, where US Marines fought in June 1918, lie 2,289 American war dead. The chapel is built over front-line trenches, and the names of 1,060 missing soldiers are carved on its walls.
new.tip: Walk up into Belleau Wood behind the cemetery, where shell holes and guns remain. The cemetery is free and run by the American Battle Monuments Commission.

new.title: Look up at the sky of words in Villers-Cotterêts
new.desc: In this Renaissance château, King François I signed the 1539 ordinance that made French the language of law and administration. Restored, it opened in November 2023 as the Cité internationale de la langue française, devoted to the French language worldwide.
new.tip: The courtyard under the glass roof, with its 'lexical sky' of suspended words, the café and the bookshop are free to enter.
new.q: Cité internationale de la langue française, Villers-Cotterêts

new.title: Meet 18th-century faces in Quentin de La Tour's pastels
new.desc: Maurice-Quentin de La Tour, pastel portraitist to the court of Louis XV, was born in Saint-Quentin. The Musée Antoine-Lécuyer holds the world's largest collection of his work, around 80 portraits glowing with life.
new.tip: The pastels are fragile, so the rooms are dimly lit: give your eyes a minute to adjust.

new.title: Glide through the marshes of the Parc d'Isle by bacôve
new.desc: Right in the middle of Saint-Quentin, the Marais d'Isle national nature reserve protects about 47 hectares of ponds and reed beds. The Maison du Parc d'Isle runs free exhibitions and boat trips in bacôves, traditional flat-bottomed punts.
new.tip: Book the boat trips at the Maison du Parc, especially the twilight ones in summer. The boardwalk observation trail is good for spotting herons.

new.title: Admire the Place Ducale in Charleville
new.desc: Duke Charles Gonzaga founded Charleville in 1606 and had Clément Métezeau design its central square, a near twin of the Place des Vosges in Paris. Arcades of brick and ochre stone with slate roofs frame a vast, harmonious square.
new.tip: Arthur Rimbaud was born a few streets away, and his museum is in the Old Mill by the Meuse nearby.

new.title: Watch the Great Puppeteer clock tell its tale
new.desc: Charleville calls itself the world capital of puppetry, and on the facade of the International Puppetry Institute a giant puppeteer automaton by Jacques Monestier performs a scene from the Ardennes legend of the Four Sons of Aymon every hour.
new.tip: On Saturday evenings all 12 episodes are played in one go. The World Puppet Theatre Festival next fills the town from 17 to 26 September 2027.

new.title: Roam the ramparts of Sedan, Europe's largest fortified castle
new.desc: Begun in 1424, Sedan's castle covers 35,000 square metres, making it the largest fortified castle in Europe. The town bought it in 1962 for a symbolic one franc, and it was voted France's favourite monument in 2023.
new.tip: Allow half a day, there are around 300 steps on the tour. In mid-May the castle hosts a big medieval festival with knights and a market.

new.title: Walk the star-shaped walls of Rocroi
new.desc: Rocroi is a whole town laid out inside a star of bastions, fortified under Francis I and Henry II in the 16th century and remodelled by Vauban in the 1670s. In 1643 the young Duke of Enghien defeated the Spanish army here, a turning point in European history.
new.tip: Follow the path along the ramparts for a full circuit. It is best seen from above, so look at an aerial photo before you go.

new.title: Count the villages from the Roche aux Sept Villages
new.desc: From a belvedere on this rocky spur between Monthermé and Bogny-sur-Meuse, you look down on the tight loops of the Meuse and the seven villages tucked into them. The site has been a protected landscape since 1957.
new.tip: There is a car park close to the viewpoint on the road from Bogny. Come early on autumn mornings when mist fills the valley.

new.title: Tour and taste at Moët & Chandon
new.desc: Founded by Claude Moët in 1743, one of the world's largest champagne houses has its headquarters on the Avenue de Champagne. Its cellars stretch for about 28 km beneath Épernay.
new.tip: Book the tour online, as walk-ins rarely get a slot in summer. The Imperial Brut makes a good benchmark to compare with smaller growers later.
new.q: Moët et Chandon, Avenue de Champagne, Épernay

new.title: Taste small-grower champagne at C. Comme in Épernay
new.desc: This bar and shop on Rue Gambetta specialises in champagnes from independent growers rather than the big houses. Its weekly tasting flights are a cheap way to compare villages and styles.
new.tip: Ask the staff for a recommendation and buy your favourite bottle at shop price downstairs.

new.title: Taste grand cru pinot noir at Champagne Mailly
new.desc: Founded in 1929 by 24 growers from the grand cru village of Mailly-Champagne, this is one of the oldest cooperatives in the region. Between 1931 and 1964 its members dug a kilometre of cellars by hand, 19 metres down in the chalk.
new.tip: Book a tasting online. Mailly's champagnes are pinot noir driven, so try the blanc de noirs.

new.title: Have lunch above the vines at the Royal Champagne
new.desc: On the slopes above Épernay at Champillon, a former coaching inn where kings stopped on their way to be crowned in Reims reopened in 2018 as a luxury hotel. Its gourmet restaurant Le Royal holds a Michelin star, and the Bellevue terrace looks straight down over the vines.
new.tip: Even if you do not stay the night, a drink on the terrace at sunset is worth the detour. Book ahead in summer.

new.title: Taste in the medieval quarries of Champagne Pannier
new.desc: In Château-Thierry, in the Aisne part of the Champagne vineyards, Pannier ages its wines in about 2 km of medieval stone quarries bought in 1937. A 14th-century archer carved into the walls, found in 2002, became the emblem of the house.
new.tip: Visits are by appointment and groups are small, so call or book ahead. Château-Thierry is the birthplace of the fabulist Jean de La Fontaine.
new.q: Champagne Pannier, Rue Roger Catillon, Château-Thierry

new.title: Sip champagne in the Gallo-Roman cellars of Joseph Perrier
new.desc: Founded in 1825, Joseph Perrier is the last champagne house still based in Châlons-en-Champagne. Its single-level cellars, dug into the hillside and of Gallo-Roman origin, run for several kilometres.
new.tip: Tastings are held at the house on Avenue de Paris. Combine it with a boat trip on the Châlons canals.
new.q: Champagne Joseph Perrier, 69 Avenue de Paris, Châlons-en-Champagne

new.title: Eat pig's trotters the Sainte-Menehould way
new.desc: Sainte-Menehould gave its name to a dish of pig's trotters simmered for hours until even the bones soften, then breaded and grilled. The hotel-restaurant Le Cheval Rouge in the town centre serves it as its house speciality.
new.tip: Eat everything, bones included, as locals do. Sainte-Menehould is also a handy stop on the way to the Valmy windmill.
new.q: Le Cheval Rouge, 1 Rue Chanzy, Sainte-Menehould

new.title: Buy Rethel white pudding from the Demoizet charcuterie
new.desc: The boudin blanc de Rethel, a delicate sausage of fresh pork, milk and eggs with no starch, has had protected status since 2001. Charcuterie Demoizet, on the main square behind Rethel's town hall, is one of the classic places to buy it.
new.tip: Pan-fry it gently in butter, never prick it. Rethel's boudin blanc fair takes place on the last Sunday of April.
new.q: Charcuterie Demoizet, Rue Hippolyte Taine, Rethel

new.title: Taste at a family grower in Hautvillers
new.desc: Champagne G. Tribaut is a family estate in Hautvillers, run by siblings who took over in 1992 and farm about 12 hectares of vines. It welcomes visitors for tastings at the property in the village where Dom Pérignon worked.
new.tip: Combine it with Dom Pérignon's grave in the abbey church nearby. Ring ahead out of season.

new.title: Ride the little train through the Mercier cellars
new.desc: Eugène Mercier dug 18 km of cellars under Épernay, and visitors tour part of them aboard a small train, 30 metres underground. In the entrance hall stands his giant barrel, shown at the 1889 Paris World Fair.
new.tip: A good choice with children or anyone who does not want to walk. Book online for the cheapest slots.
new.q: Maison Mercier, 68 Avenue de Champagne, Épernay

new.title: Climb the 237 steps of the Castellane tower
new.desc: At 66 metres, the tower of the de Castellane house is the highest point in Épernay, built in the early 1900s by architect Marius Toudoire. The climb ends with a 360° panorama over the town and the vineyards of the Marne valley.
new.tip: Combine the tower with a cellar tour and tasting. It is open from spring to December.

new.title: Join the Habits de Lumière festival in Épernay
new.desc: Every December since 2000, Épernay lights up the Avenue de Champagne for three days of illuminations, video mapping, champagne bars and fireworks. The 2026 edition runs from 11 to 13 December.
new.tip: Book accommodation early or come for the evening by train from Reims. Wrap up warm and buy a glass at the pop-up champagne bars.
new.q: Hôtel de Ville, Avenue de Champagne, Épernay

new.title: Float along the Mau and Nau canals of Châlons
new.desc: Châlons-en-Champagne is threaded with small rivers and canals, and the tourist office runs boat trips along them under old bridges and past the Grand Jard park. The night version, Métamorph'eau'ses, adds a sound and light show.
new.tip: Book at the tourist office on Quai des Arts, where the boats leave. The night trip is the highlight in summer.

new.title: Watch thousands of cranes at the Lac du Der
new.desc: The Lac du Der-Chantecoq, one of the largest artificial lakes in France, is a major stopover for migrating common cranes. Each autumn tens of thousands roost here, with 60,000 counted at the end of October 2026.
new.tip: Be on the dikes at dawn or dusk to see the flocks fly out or come in. The LPO runs guided outings on Tuesday and Friday evenings in late autumn.

new.title: Cycle the Trans-Ardennes greenway along the Meuse
new.desc: The Voie Verte Trans-Ardennes follows the Meuse for about 130 km from Mouzon through Charleville-Mézières to Givet on the Belgian border, part of the EuroVelo 19 route. The finest stretch winds through steep wooded gorges and slate villages around Monthermé.
new.tip: Monthermé is a good base, with the river loops on both sides. Trains along the valley let you ride one way and return by rail.

new.title: Paddle a canoe down the Semoy valley
new.desc: The Semoy winds through a deep, wooded valley before joining the Meuse at Monthermé. Canoë Semoy, based at the campsite in Haulmé, rents canoes, kayaks and paddleboards with all the gear included.
new.tip: Booking is recommended in summer and you need to be able to swim. Pack a picnic for a riverside stop.
